items.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I talked the Weiss brothers into recording Red Norvo’s trio

ctx.x: At the Haig, yeah. They hired me six nights a week. Red Norvo was playing on the off nights, with Tal Farlow and Charlie Mingus and Red, which was one of my favorite groups. I had just started Fantasy Records, so I talked the Weiss brothers into recording Red Norvo’s trio, which I think is some of the greatest small combo recordings ever made. I talked them into recording Gerry. Gerry said I gave him his first steady job by moving him into the Blackhawk. Then Red Norvo came up there. But I still had to work.…
Let me ask you about a couple of other things that happened around this time. Is it true that you taught an extension course on the history of jazz at U. C. Berkeley?

items.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewer states 'I remember I met Max Weiss' and quotes him; the interviewee (Dave Brubeck) does not claim a personal relationship with Max Weiss.

ctx.x: When you’d be in the studio, and somebody would say, “Okay. Let’s go over this garbage,” it’s no way to feel good about what you were about to do. Your mood in studios – you want to have a certain dignity. The word “garbage” always stuck in my mind.

I remember I met Max Weiss. I did a long interview with him. He told me, “I’m not a jazz guy. I’ve never been a jazz guy. My philosophy is, you can’t fall in love with the product. It’s just a product.”

That’s a good description. Sol Weiss must have been an excellent recording engineer, because those old trio things are so well done. Sometimes I think with maybe one microphone. Now it takes us seven mics on the drums, balance, and all that.
